A stopper at the end of a rope, and the start of many other knots.
Make a loop, the end crossing over the standing part.
Bring the end round behind and up through the loop. Pull both ends tight.
A bigger stopper than the overhand, and easier to untie.
Make a loop, the end crossing over the standing part.
Take the end round behind the standing part.
Pass it down through the loop from the front. Pull tight; it should look like an 8.
A strong fixed loop that won\'t slip, at the end of a rope or in the middle.
Fold the rope to make a long bight.
Tie a figure-eight with the doubled rope, leaving the fold as the loop. Keep the strands side by side and pull tight.
A fixed loop at the end of a rope that holds under load and unties easily after.
Make a small loop in the standing part, the side toward the end lying on top. Leave enough rope for the big loop.
Bring the end up through the small loop and round behind the standing part.
Take it back down through the small loop, beside itself. Hold the end and the loop side together and pull the standing part.
Ties a rope to a post or rail quickly, and is easy to adjust. It can work loose if the pull keeps changing.
Wrap the end round the post.
Cross it over itself and wrap round again.
Tuck the end under that last crossing. Pull both ends.
Ties a rope to a ring, post or tree, and holds under a steady pull.
Take the end round the post and back beside the standing part.
Pass it over the standing part, round behind it, and out under itself. That is one half hitch.
Make a second the same way, a little further along. Slide them snug.
An adjustable loop for tent and tarp guylines: slide it to tighten, and it holds.
Take the end round the stake and back beside the line.
Wrap it twice round the line, working back toward the stake, inside the loop.
Bring it out across the wraps and make one more turn round the line outside them, tucked under itself. Slide the knot to tighten.
Joins two ropes, even of different thickness.
Fold a bight in the thicker rope.
Bring the other end up through the bight and round behind both of its legs.
Cross it over the bight and tuck it under its own standing part. Pull tight.
Ties the two ends of one cord round something, like a bandage or a bundle. Not for joining ropes that will take a load.
Right over left: cross the ends and tuck one under.
Left over right: cross them the other way and tuck again. Each end comes out beside its own part.
Pull both pairs of ends tight.
A loop of thinner cord that grips a rope when loaded and slides when not: for a sliding anchor or hauling.
Lay the cord loop behind the rope and pass one end of it round the rope and through the other end.
Do it twice more, three wraps in all, inside the first. Dress the wraps flat and side by side, and load it to test the grip.
Joins two ropes securely, or makes a loop of cord for a prusik. Hard to untie after a load.
Lay the two ends side by side, pointing opposite ways. Wrap one end twice round both ropes, then pass it back through the wraps.
Do the same with the other end, the other way.
Pull the standing parts so the two knots slide together.
Drags or lifts a log or pole. Holds while pulled and falls off when slack.
Pass the end round the log.
Take it round the standing part.
Twist it round its own part three times. Pull the standing part so the turns bite.
